title: The Protection Diode That Starved the 5 V Sensor
featured_title: THE PROTECTION DIODE THAT STARVED THE 5 V SENSOR
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

presentation.challenge: The reverse-polarity protection worked, but the 5 V sensor would not start.

practice.primary_question: Why can a forward-biased protection diode make a downstream 5 V sensor fail even though the source is correct?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating a forward-biased silicon diode as a perfect zero-volt short when supply margin matters.

case_dna.target_misconception: A forward-biased silicon diode can always be replaced by an ideal zero-volt short without affecting supply-margin calculations.
case_dna.why_plausible: The ideal-diode model is useful for state reasoning, so its zero-drop assumption is easy to over-apply.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Using a 0.7 V drop, the protected 5.0 V rail becomes about 4.3 V, below the sensor minimum.
case_dna.corrected_model: Choose the diode model that matches the design question and include forward voltage when margin matters.

problem_statement: A 5.0 V source feeds a sensor through a series silicon diode for reverse-polarity protection. The sensor requires at least 4.5 V to start. The design review assumes a forward-biased diode is simply ON, but the measured sensor rail is only 4.3 V. Diagnose the missing diode model and choose a correction that preserves protection and restores voltage margin.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The reverse-polarity protection worked, but the 5 V sensor would not start.
facts: Series silicon diode: 0.7 V forward-drop model
gates.prompt: What did the protection diode change in the powered circuit?

gates.label: Theory
gates.heading: Choose the diode model before calculating the sensor rail

options.label: A forward-biased diode is an ideal short, so the sensor still receives 5.0 V
options.reason: The ideal-diode model ignores forward drop.

options.label: The diode drops about 0.7 V, leaving about 4.3 V for the sensor
A forward-biased diode behaves as an open circuit
options.reason: A conducting forward-biased diode is not open.

options.label: The diode adds 0.7 V to the sensor rail
options.reason: The forward drop subtracts from the supply.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the sensor supply voltage
gates.prompt: Using a 0.7 V forward drop, what voltage reaches the sensor from a 5.0 V source?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Power the protected rail
gates.result: The sensor rail settles at about 4.3 V, below the 4.5 V startup requirement.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the missing voltage
gates.success: Vsensor = 4.3 V, below the 4.5 V requirement.
gates.hint: The diode is in series with the sensor supply.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The diode model explains the startup failure

cards.text: The conducting silicon diode is modeled with about 0.7 V across it.
The remaining sensor rail is 4.3 V, below the 4.5 V minimum.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the protection review
report: C2. A silicon diode is placed in series for reverse-polarity protection.
C3. Because the diode is forward biased, the sensor still receives the full 5.0 V.

evidence_choices.label: 5.0 V - 0.7 V = 4.3 V at the sensor rail
evidence_choices.reason: This directly shows the lost voltage margin.

evidence_choices.label: The diode blocks reverse polarity
evidence_choices.reason: That is its protection function, not the undervoltage evidence.

correction.template: With the silicon protection diode conducting, the sensor rail is about {rail_v} V, not 5.0 V.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Keep protection and meet the 4.5 V sensor minimum
gates.constraint: Keep the 5.0 V source and series-diode style protection.

options.label: Use a diode with about 0.3 V forward drop
Keep the 0.7 V diode because ON means zero volts
Add a second 0.7 V silicon diode in series

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the series-drop rule
gates.prompt: A 3.3 V rail feeds a load through a 0.3 V forward-biased diode. Approximately what voltage reaches the load?
gates.explanation: A conducting series diode reduces the downstream rail by its forward drop.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the diode-model correction
gates.confirmation: I confirm that diode forward voltage must be included when checking downstream supply margin.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The sensor rail fell to about 4.3 V.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: Forward biased was treated as a zero-volt short.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Include the forward drop when checking supply margin.

seo.seo_title: Diode Forward Voltage Drop: Why a 5 V Rail Becomes 4.3 V | FE E-026
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-026: a 5 V sensor rail falls to 4.3 V through a silicon protection diode. Diagnose the forward-voltage drop and restore supply margin.
seo.focus_keyphrase: diode forward voltage drop FE exam
seo.excerpt: A forward-biased diode can conduct correctly and still remove enough voltage to make a downstream circuit fail.
seo.direct_answer: In the constant-drop model, a forward-biased silicon diode drops about 0.7 V. A 5.0 V source feeding a load through that diode therefore leaves about 4.3 V at the load.

faqs.q: What voltage remains after a 0.7 V diode drop from 5 V?
Is a forward-biased silicon diode always a perfect short?
faqs.a: No. The ideal model treats it that way, but the constant-drop model includes forward voltage.
